title: ArrayList internal working — dynamic array, 1.5x growth, resize, initial capacity

s1_definition.profdef: ArrayList internally uses `Object[] elementData` — a plain Java array. Default initial capacity: **10**. When the array is full and you add another element, ArrayList creates a NEW array of size `oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1)` = **1.5x** the old capacity (10→15→22→33→49...), copies all elements via `Arrays.copyOf()` (which uses `System.arraycopy()` — native, fast), and inserts the new element. This is called **resizing/growing**. You can set initial capacity via `new ArrayList<>(1000)` to avoid repeated resizing when you know the approximate size. `trimToSize()` shrinks the array to the current size (reclaims wasted memory). `ensureCapacity(n)` pre-allocates to avoid repeated grows.
s1_definition.analogy: ArrayList is like a bank's account REGISTER BOOK with numbered pages. Starts with 10 pages (default capacity). When all 10 are filled: buy a BIGGER book (1.5x = 15 pages), photocopy all 10 pages into the new book, add the 11th entry. The old book is thrown away (garbage collected). If you KNOW you'll have 1000 accounts: buy a 1000-page book upfront (`new ArrayList<>(1000)`) — avoids buying bigger books 20 times.
s1_definition.oneliner: ArrayList = Object[] array. Default capacity 10. Grows 1.5x when full (copy all elements). Set initial capacity to avoid resizing: `new ArrayList<>(expectedSize)`.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** ArrayList internally uses `Object[] elementData` — a plain Java array. Default initial capacity: **10**. When the array is full and you add another element, ArrayList creates a NEW array of size `oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1)` = **1.5x** the old capacity (10→15→22→33→49...), copies all elements via `Arrays.copyOf()` (which uses `System.arraycopy()` — native, fast), and inserts the new element. This is called **resizing/growing**. You can set initial capacity via `new ArrayList<>(1000)` to avoid repeated resizing when you know the approximate size. `trimToSize()` shrinks the array to the current size (reclaims wasted memory). `ensureCapacity(n)` pre-allocates to avoid repeated grows.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** ArrayList is like a bank's account REGISTER BOOK with numbered pages. Starts with 10 pages (default capacity). When all 10 are filled: buy a BIGGER book (1.5x = 15 pages), photocopy all 10 pages into the new book, add the 11th entry. The old book is thrown away (garbage collected). If you KNOW you'll have 1000 accounts: buy a 1000-page book upfront (`new ArrayList<>(1000)`) — avoids buying bigger books 20 times.

**One line to remember:** ArrayList = Object[] array. Default capacity 10. Grows 1.5x when full (copy all elements). Set initial capacity to avoid resizing: `new ArrayList<>(expectedSize)`.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The EOD batch loaded 2 million account records into `new ArrayList<>()`.** Default capacity 10 → grew 1.5x repeatedly → 40+ resize operations → 40 array copies of increasing size → 3.2 seconds wasted on resizing alone. Fix: `new ArrayList<>(2_000_000)` — ONE allocation, zero resizes. Batch load time: 4.5s → 1.3s.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is account transactions added to an `ArrayList` backed by a dynamic array.

**Step 1.** Each `add` writes the transaction into the next free slot of the internal array and increments the size counter in O(1).

**Step 2.** When the array is full, the list calls `grow()`, which allocates a new array 1.5 times the old capacity and uses `Arrays.copyOf` to move all elements.

**Step 3.** Giving an initial capacity up front (for example `new ArrayList<>(1000)`) avoids these repeated copies, and `get(index)` always returns Rajesh's entry in O(1) by direct array indexing.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ ArrayList GROWTH ═══

  add("A"): capacity 0 → allocate 10 → [A][_][_][_][_][_][_][_][_][_]
  add("B"): [A][B][_][_][_][_][_][_][_][_]
  ...
  add(10th): [A][B][C][D][E][F][G][H][I][J]  ← FULL!
  add(11th): grow! newCapacity = 10 + 10>>1 = 15
             new Object[15], copy 10 elements
             [A][B][C][D][E][F][G][H][I][J][K][_][_][_][_]
  ...
  add(16th): grow! 15 + 15>>1 = 22
  add(23rd): grow! 22 + 22>>1 = 33

  ═══ COST OF RESIZING ═══
  Each resize: allocate new array + System.arraycopy (all elements)
  For 1M elements with default capacity: ~40 resizes!
  For 1M elements with capacity(1M): ZERO resizes! (Recommended) 

  ═══ size vs capacity ═══
  list.size() = 2 (elements stored)
  capacity    = 50 (array length — internal, not exposed via API)
  trimToSize() → capacity shrinks to size
```

```
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   Transaction Log Store (Bank) — ArrayList      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        │ append txn (O(1) amortized)
        ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ Object[] elementData          │  index access O(1)
  │ [T0][T1][T2][ ][ ][ ][ ][ ]   │

    trimToSize() → reclaim unused slots after bulk load
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
ArrayList internally uses `Object[] elementData`. Default capacity is 10 (lazy — allocated on first add). When full, it grows by 1.5x: `newCapacity = oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1)` → 10→15→22→33→49. Growth involves allocating a new array and copying ALL elements via `System.arraycopy()` (native, fast, but still O(n)). For known sizes: `new ArrayList<>(expectedSize)` avoids repeated resizing — critical for bulk loads.

`size()` returns the number of elements stored. Capacity is the internal array length (not exposed via API). `trimToSize()` shrinks capacity to match size — useful after bulk loading to reclaim wasted memory. `ensureCapacity(n)` pre-grows to avoid multiple small resizes. In banking: EOD batch loading 2M records — without initial capacity: ~40 resizes, wasted seconds. With `new ArrayList<>(2_000_000)`: one allocation, zero resizes, 3x faster load. Always set initial capacity when you know (or can estimate) the final size.

---

keyPoints: Backed by a dynamic Object[] array
Grows by ~50% when full (1.5x) — copies old array to new larger one
get(index) is O(1), add at end is amortized O(1), insert in middle is O(n)
